slides.title: Appendix D — Working Glossary and Acceptance Review
keyPoints: Vocabulary must support algorithm reasoning
Acceptance review ties claims to witnesses
Definitions are not enough without edge cases
slides.narration: Welcome to Appendix D. This is where algorithm vocabulary becomes a review instrument. Learners should not merely define abstraction, invariant, frontier, stability, or sentinel. They should use those words to explain a concrete implementation decision, a failure mode, and the evidence that proves the implementation satisfies its contract.

comparisons.label: Abstraction
comparisons.text: A model exposing relevant operations and guarantees while hiding some implementation details. A queue abstraction defines FIFO behavior; a ring buffer is one possible representation of it. The abstraction should not promise guarantees the representation does not maintain.

comparisons.label: Invariant
comparisons.text: A property maintained at a designated boundary, such as before every loop iteration or after every public mutation. An invariant is useful when it explains what the representation means and supports the next operation, not merely when it restates that the program should work.

comparisons.label: Comparator equivalence
comparisons.text: Two values are equivalent under an ordering when neither compares before the other. This can differ from operator==. Ordered containers and sorting stability must be understood in terms of the comparator actually supplied.

comparisons.label: Partition boundary
comparisons.text: A position dividing a sequence according to a predicate. Lower-bound search returns such a boundary; it does not by itself prove that a matching element exists at that position.

slides.title: Review an implementation before relying on it
keyPoints: Write the public contract in ordinary language and make the error model visible. State the accepted sizes.
State the public contract
Separate edge cases from ordinary missing results
Record exact witnesses
slides.narration: Acceptance review forces the algorithm out of vague correctness. Write the public contract in ordinary language and make the error model visible. State the accepted sizes, duplicate policy, ordering assumptions, graph direction, arithmetic bounds, and ownership relationships. Include the meaning of empty input and missing results. A precise small contract is more useful than a broad promise the implementation cannot defend. Require learners to name accepted inputs, rejected inputs, duplicate policy, ordering assumptions, graph direction, arithmetic bounds, and ownership relationships. Then require the witness: exact output, assertion, test fixture, trace, benchmark, or diagnostic.

question.prompt: What should an acceptance review refuse to accept?

slides.narration: Close with a five-term evidence drill. Learners choose five algorithm vocabulary terms and write one sentence for each that names a source-level mechanism and an observable witness. The point is not elegant prose. The point is technical language that survives contact with code, edge cases, and measurement.
